related_questions.question: Why am I getting rashes all of a sudden?

text_blocks.snippet: A sudden rash can be caused by a variety of factors, including allergic reactions, irritants, infections, or underlying skin conditions. It's important to identify the potential cause to determine the appropriate treatment and whether to seek medical advice.
snippet_highlighted_words: allergic reactions, irritants, infections, or underlying skin conditions

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a breakdown of common causes:

list.title: Contact Dermatitis:
list.snippet: This is a reaction to something that has touched your skin, like a new soap, lotion, or even a plant like poison ivy.

list.title: Hives (Urticaria):
list.snippet: These are itchy, raised, red welts that can be triggered by various allergens, including foods, medications, insect bites, or even stress.

list.title: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis):
list.snippet: This chronic condition often appears as red, itchy, and scaly patches, and can be linked to allergies or asthma.

list.title: Psoriasis:
list.snippet: This condition can cause red, scaly patches, particularly over joints and along the scalp.

list.title: Seborrheic Dermatitis:
list.snippet: This rash appears in patches around the eyebrows, eyelids, nose, and ears, and can cause dandruff on the scalp.

list.title: Viral or Bacterial Infections:
list.snippet: Some rashes are a symptom of infections, like impetigo (bacterial) or chickenpox (viral).

list.title: Fungal Infections:
list.snippet: Ringworm and athlete's foot are examples of fungal infections that can cause rashes.
Irritants: Exposure to harsh chemicals, detergents, or even certain fabrics can cause a rash.
Heat: Heat rashes occur when sweat gets trapped under the skin, causing irritation and bumps.
Stress: Stress can trigger or worsen existing rashes like hives.
Medications: Some medications can cause skin reactions as a side effect.
If the rash is spreading rapidly or involves large areas of the body .
If the rash is painful or accompanied by other symptoms like fever, blistering, or difficulty breathing .
If you suspect a severe allergic reaction .
If the rash doesn't improve with home care within a week or two .

text_blocks.snippet: To help identify the cause of your rash, consider these questions:

list.snippet: What does the rash look like (color, texture, shape)?
Where on your body is it located?
When did it start?
Are you experiencing any other symptoms?
Have you been exposed to any new substances or medications?
Do you have any known allergies?
Do you have a history of skin conditions like eczema or psoriasis?
